opus-5.5.text:
I think it helps to separate two different kinds of generalization, because those two tasks are actually showing off different things.

For table clearing, or bussing, the generalization is mostly about **breadth of environment and objects**. You walk into a new home or a new table setup, and there are cups, plates, utensils, food scraps, wrappers. Many of these specific items the robot has never seen. The table height is different, the lighting is different, the clutter is arranged differently. What's impressive is that the policy still has a reasonable notion of what "clearing" means: trash goes in the bin, dishes go in the bus tub. It handles a long tail of objects without anyone engineering a category for each one. I'd call that semantic and visual generalization. The model carries a kind of common sense about objects that comes partly from pretraining on web-scale vision-language data and partly from seeing a lot of diverse robot data.

Clothes folding is a different beast. The objects are fairly constrained, it's shirts, shorts, towels. But each one is **deformable**, and every time you drop it on the table it lands in a totally different configuration. There's no fixed state you can plan from. So the generalization there is more about **dexterity and closed-loop behavior**: recovering when a fold goes wrong, flattening something that's crumpled, regrasping when the cloth slips. You can't script that. The policy has to react continuously to what it sees. That's why folding was such a meaningful milestone for us. It's less "I've never seen this object" and more "I've never seen this exact state, and I need to make progress from it anyway."

So roughly, bussing tests *what* the robot can understand, and folding tests *how* the robot can act. And the interesting part about putting both under one model is the hypothesis that these aren't separate skills you build separately. If you train on enough diverse data across many tasks and many robot embodiments, the model learns a shared foundation. Some of the physical intuition from one task transfers to others, the same way language models picked up broad abilities from broad data.

I also want to be honest about the limits. When we say "generalization," it's still fairly local. The robot can handle new instances of tasks it has been trained on, in new settings. It doesn't mean you can hand it a completely new task, with zero data, and expect it to work reliably. Robustness is still a big issue too. A demo that succeeds most of the time is very different from something you'd trust in someone's home every day. Closing that gap, from "it often works" to "it basically always works," is in my view where a lot of the real research is now.

r001.rationale: It says garments land in different configurations and the policy must make progress from an exact state it has never seen, conveying generalization to configurations absent from its examples.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes the constrained garment types (shirts, shorts, towels) from the many possible configurations each garment can take.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. I think the first thing to say is that those two demos are actually showing two different kinds of generalization, and people tend to lump them together.

Table-clearing is mostly what I'd call object-level and scene-level generalization. The robot has seen a lot of trash, a lot of dishes, a lot of cluttered tables in training, but the specific configuration in front of it is new. The cup is at a different angle, the napkin is partly under the plate, the lighting is different. So what the policy has to do is recognize the category of thing, pick an appropriate grasp, and keep executing a sequence of pick-and-place steps without losing track of the goal. That's generalization across instances within a distribution the model has basically covered. It's impressive, but it's closer to what we expect from a well-trained vision-language backbone. The language model part gives it the semantic prior that a crumpled napkin is trash and a bowl is not, and the flow-matching action head turns that into smooth continuous motion. The hard part there is really the long horizon, not any single grasp.

Clothes-folding is a different animal. The object is deformable, which means the state space is enormous and you can't really define a fixed "pose" of a shirt. Every fold you make changes the geometry for the next step. So the kind of generalization that matters is more like generalization over dynamics and recovery. If a sleeve flips the wrong way, the policy has to notice that from vision and improvise a correction rather than replaying a memorized trajectory. When you watch the longer videos, that's what stands out to me, not the folding itself but the number of times it gets something slightly wrong and fixes it. That kind of robustness comes from training on a lot of messy, imperfect demonstrations, including the corrections, rather than on clean ones.

The honest caveat is that both tasks are still within the training distribution in a broad sense. Pi Zero was trained on thousands of hours of exactly these household tasks across a fleet of robots. So I'd describe it as strong interpolation, with some genuine extrapolation in object instances and in error recovery. What we haven't really seen yet is the model handling a task category it was never shown, where you'd want the language understanding to bootstrap entirely new motor behavior. That's the test that would tell us whether the "foundation model" framing for robotics is actually earned, and I don't think the folding and clearing demos answer it yet. They answer a narrower but still important question, which is whether a single policy with one set of weights can cover many tasks and many embodiments without falling apart. And on that question, the answer looks like yes.

r001.rationale: The response describes handling changing shirt geometry and correcting mistakes, but does not say successful folding requires generalizing to garment configurations absent from the collected data. It instead characterizes the demos as broadly within the training distribution.

r002.rationale: The response discusses garment configurations and recovery, but does not identify generalization across garment categories as a distinct dimension.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish a few kinds of generalization. In table-clearing, you can vary the objects, their positions, and the clutter. The question is whether the robot can still carry out a familiar task when the particular scene is unfamiliar. That’s different from learning an entirely new task.

Clothes-folding adds another dimension: the object changes shape as you manipulate it. Even the same shirt can start in many different configurations, so the robot has to respond to what it sees as it acts, rather than simply replay a fixed sequence.

But the task names alone don’t tell us how strong the generalization is. Were those objects, garments, or configurations represented in training? How different were the test conditions? I’d interpret these tasks as evidence to investigate generalization within a task, while being careful not to equate that with an ability to handle arbitrary new tasks.

r001.rationale: It says a shirt may start in many configurations and asks whether those configurations were represented in training, but does not state that successful folding requires generalizing to configurations absent from collected data.

r002.rationale: It discusses varying configurations of the same shirt, but does not identify generalization across garment categories as a distinct dimension.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish a few kinds of generalization. In table clearing, the robot encounters different objects, arrangements, and clutter. It has to carry what it learned into a scene that doesn’t look exactly like its training examples, while still figuring out what to pick up and how to grasp it.

Clothes folding adds another dimension: the object itself changes shape as you act on it. A shirt can start in many configurations, and each action changes what the next action should be. So the policy has to keep responding to what it sees, rather than replaying a fixed sequence.

But we should be careful about what those demonstrations establish. Handling a new arrangement or a new garment within a familiar task is different from learning an entirely new task. The interesting question is which parts of the situation are new, and how far they are from the training experience. Those examples suggest useful flexibility, but by themselves they don’t establish unrestricted generalization.

r001.rationale: The response says shirts can start in many configurations, but does not say those configurations were absent from the collected data.

r002.rationale: It discusses garment configurations but does not identify generalization across garment categories as a separate dimension.
